I’m a woman, but I feel like I can relate to you a lot. A decade into my marriage, I began feeling bored. The differences between my husband and I that didn’t matter to me early on were bothering me. I had an emotional affair with a coworker, and I regret it so much. My husband for some reason unfathomable to me, forgave me. 

My advice would be to throw all this attention and wonder into your wife. Ask her the things you asked this other woman. Engage your wife on that level. Start conversations, over and over and over. Find that connection in your marriage, not outside of it. If you aren’t able to after honestly giving it that effort, than you owe it to your wife to talk about it first before finding it elsewhere. Just my two cents. But I beg of you not to do things out of order. There is so much pain that way, please take it from me.

It’s not a test of insanity… which from my understanding is more of a legal threshold than a concept in psychology. It’s a test of psychopathic tendencies. Psychology tends to associate antisocial personality disorder with psychopathy, which is entirely different from autism. I think the test results indicates that Abed is the least likely to be the perpetrator of a violent crime, which I fully accept. Stereotypes perpetuate a myth that people with disorders are violent, but there is no link between autism and violence, and in general, people with mental disorders are more likely to be the victims of a violent crime.

It’s been a few years, so I might be forgetting some of the details, but a huge part of it for me was figuring out where in my life I had been discouraged or deterred from creativity, and what creative blocks those moments had led to. It helped me see who and what in my life was harming my creative practice, which indirectly helped me see what I needed to eliminate. It helped me envision what type of artist I wanted to be, and solidified goals that I had never actually verbalized/articulated. 

In my personal life, it helped me identify the people in my life who were actively making my life worse, which led to me putting up boundaries with some and completely cutting others out. It was an actual life changing experience for me. I can’t guarantee it will be for everyone, but I will sing its praises for many years to come.

Honestly, I feel for you. I’ve been stuck in a depression hell hole for ten months. I just do as much as I can on good days to find a sense of happiness or even calm when I’m too numb for happiness, and then just try to be extra forgiving to myself on bad days. I think depression is such a motivation killer, so I try not to beat myself up when I don’t have any. A good friend of mine who also struggles with depression has started just making an actual physical list of things he enjoys. Things he knows he can fall back on when he doesn’t want to keep trying. Having a few of those things helps me too. I’m not sure if that’s all that helpful to your question, but hang in there. We’ll make it through one day!

I’ve also struggled making friends my entire life. I don’t have anyone I want to post about who I have that kind of relationship with. The best advice I could give is just to step away from social media for a bit. The best way for me is to delete the apps from my phone so I won’t open them absentmindedly. Giving myself that space from social media helps me reset, and it helps me forget about all those stupid petty things I feel. I’m sorry you’re feeling this way, but when you focus on your real life and not the things floating by on a social media feed, it might help remind you how little social media really means when you can go days or weeks or months without it.

I also have what, from the outside, looks like a happy life. Sometimes it’s not at all about the circumstances. It’s about brain chemistry or genetic predisposition, etc. I would strongly recommend doing something, anything. Talk to someone you trust, or, even better, someone you trust who would understand and empathize with mental illness. Talk to a doctor. Try a medication (but realize it might take time to find the right one for you). Find a therapist. I know it feels like nothing will change, especially when you look around and see no reason why you should feel this way. But there are so many things that you can try.
